questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with bronchiectasis has 3 months of increasing breathlessness and ankle swelling. She produces a cup of green sputum daily. Her JVP is raised 5 cm, there is a loud P2 and pitting oedema to the mid-shin. Her oxygen saturation is 89% breathing air. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle with normal left ventricular function.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic lung disease (here bronchiectasis) is cor pulmonale.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: dilated right ventricle with normal left ventricular function
steps.x: Chronic lung disease with right heart failure signs and a loud P2.

elim: Would not cause a loud P2 or a dilated right ventricle with lung disease.
Causes oedema but not a raised JVP or loud P2.
Rare, rheumatic, and would not explain the loud P2.

steps.x: B: Cor pulmonale. Lung disease + PH + right heart failure = cor pulmonale.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has 1 year of progressive breathlessness and tiredness. She had a ventricular septal defect as a child that was never repaired. She now has central cyanosis and finger clubbing. Her oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air. There is a loud P2 and the previous loud murmur has become much quieter.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
questions.e: An uncorrected left-to-right shunt causes pulmonary hypertension; the loud P2 and quieter murmur reflect rising pulmonary pressures.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
Congenital heart disease with progressive symptoms, cyanosis and a loud P2.

elim: Does not cause cyanosis, clubbing and a loud P2.
No fever or new murmur; the murmur has become quieter.
Does not cause cyanosis or a loud P2.
Progressive over a year with congenital heart disease, not acute.

steps.x: E: Pulmonary hypertension. Congenital heart disease is a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thromboembolic disease is seen in clinic. Her JVP is raised 4 cm and she has mild ankle oedema. On auscultation the second heart sound is split with a loud pulmonary component, and there is a second murmur.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on auscultation?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
Slow-rising pulse with a soft second heart sound
questions.e: A dilated pulmonary valve ring causes pulmonary regurgitation: an early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely additional finding on auscultation?
Pulmonary hypertension signs with an extra murmur.

elim: Aortic stenosis, with a soft not loud S2.

steps.x: A: Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge. PH signs: raised JVP, oedema, loud P2, early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with interstitial lung disease has 6 months of worsening breathlessness and fainted while walking uphill last week. He has fine bibasal crackles and clubbing. His pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There is no murmur. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: T wave inversion in V1 to V3 and the inferior leads: right ventricular strain.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Exertional syncope and breathlessness with right ventricular strain in a patient with lung disease is pulmonary hypertension.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Chronic lung disease, exertional syncope and right heart strain on ECG.

elim: No murmur, and the ECG shows right not left ventricular strain.
Progressive over 6 months, not a sudden collapse with shock.
Exertional syncope with right heart strain is never vasovagal.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary hypertension. Exertional syncope + lung disease + RV strain = pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with pulmonary hypertension from COPD has 2 days of palpitations and worse breathlessness. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 128 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Her JVP is raised and she has ankle oedema. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which complication of her pulmonary hypertension has she developed?
questions.e: Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation complicate pulmonary hypertension as the right atrium dilates.

steps.x: The question asks: Which complication of her pulmonary hypertension has she developed?
Irregularly irregular pulse in pulmonary hypertension.

elim: Would be regular at about 150 bpm with sawtooth waves.

steps.x: A: Atrial fibrillation. Complications of PH: right heart failure, syncope, arrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman is reviewed in a pulmonary hypertension clinic. Two years ago she had only breathlessness on hills and tiredness. She now gets breathless walking across a room. The consultant says her disease has entered a late stage.
questions.q: Which finding is most likely to show that her disease is now advanced?
o: Peripheral oedema with a raised JVP
questions.e: Right heart failure (raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly) is a late sign of pulmonary hypertension.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding is most likely to show that her disease is now advanced?
The question asks for a LATE sign.

elim: Present early once pulmonary pressures rise.

steps.x: E: Peripheral oedema with a raised JVP. Right heart failure is a late sign of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy has worsening breathlessness. He has orthopnoea and bibasal crackles. He has never smoked and has no history of thromboembolism. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 55 mmHg. Spirometry is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pulmonary hypertension?
questions.e: Severe left ventricular dysfunction raises left-sided filling pressure and pulmonary pressure: PH due to left heart disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his pulmonary hypertension?
Severe LV impairment with raised pulmonary pressure.

elim: He has never smoked and spirometry is normal.
Rare, and there is an obvious cause.
Crackles here are from pulmonary oedema; the left ventricle is severely impaired.

steps.x: E: Left heart disease. Left heart disease is a common cause of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 9 months of progressive breathlessness and a loud P2. Her oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air and her lungs are clear. A chest X-ray is requested before echocardiography. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral prominent hila from enlarged pulmonary arteries.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning
Kerley B lines with upper lobe diversion
Unilateral pleural effusion with a meniscus
questions.e: Raised pulmonary arterial pressure enlarges the central pulmonary arteries (prominent hila) while peripheral vessels look pruned.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
Suspected PH; the X-ray supports, the echo assesses.

elim: Pulmonary oedema from left heart failure.
Not a feature of pulmonary hypertension.

steps.x: B: Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning. PH on CXR: big proximal pulmonary arteries, pruned peripheries.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has 8 months of breathlessness on stairs and chest tightness when she hurries. She has had three pulmonary emboli in the past 4 years. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is a loud P2 and a raised JVP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Progressive breathlessness and chest pain with a loud P2 after recurrent PEs is pulmonary hypertension.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Recurrent PEs with progressive symptoms and a loud P2.

elim: Does not cause a loud P2 and raised JVP.
No wheeze; does not cause a loud P2.
Would cause an ejection systolic murmur, not a loud P2.
She has no syncope and has right heart signs.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary hypertension. Recurrent PE history + progressive breathlessness + loud P2 = pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with pulmonary hypertension due to interstitial lung disease has 2 weeks of increasing leg swelling and a 4 kg weight gain. He has right upper quadrant discomfort. His JVP is raised 7 cm and his liver is enlarged and tender. His lungs have fine crackles unchanged from before. Albumin and liver enzymes are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised JVP, oedema and tender hepatomegaly in pulmonary hypertension are right heart failure from RV failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: Albumin and liver enzymes are normal
steps.x: Right-sided congestion on a background of PH.

elim: Normal albumin and liver enzymes; a raised JVP points to the heart.
Bilateral swelling with a raised JVP is not a DVT.
His crackles are unchanged and he has right-sided signs.

steps.x: E: Right heart failure. PH complications: right heart failure (cor pulmonale), syncope, arrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after recurrent pulmonary emboli. He is breathless on mild exertion with a raised JVP and loud P2. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and regular. A 12-lead ECG is recorded at his clinic visit.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
o: Bifid P waves in lead II
Delta waves with a short PR interval
Saddle-shaped ST elevation in all leads
Tall peaked P waves in lead II
Tall R waves in V5 and V6 with left axis
questions.e: Right atrial enlargement from pulmonary hypertension causes P pulmonale: tall, peaked P waves.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
Pulmonary hypertension, so right atrial changes.

elim: P mitrale, from left atrial enlargement.

steps.x: D: Tall peaked P waves in lead II. P pulmonale (tall peaked P) = right atrial enlargement in PH.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 2 years of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He has never smoked and has no history of thromboembolism. He has finger clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.85 with a reduced FVC. Echocardiography shows a raised estimated pulmonary artery pressure with normal left ventricular function.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pulmonary hypertension?
questions.e: Restrictive spirometry, clubbing and fine crackles point to interstitial lung disease as the cause of his PH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his pulmonary hypertension?
Restrictive lung disease with PH.

elim: Never smoked and spirometry is restrictive, not obstructive.
Rare; there is an obvious lung cause.

steps.x: D: Interstitial lung disease. Lung disease (COPD, ILD) is a common cause of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with COPD is admitted with increasing ankle swelling. His JVP is raised 5 cm, there is a loud P2 and pitting oedema to the knees. His oxygen saturation is 88% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with no consolidation. The team suspects pulmonary hypertension.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Echocardiography is the initial investigation, estimating pulmonary artery pressure and showing RV size and function.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Suspected PH: need a first non-invasive test.

elim: A supporting test for thromboembolic disease, not first-line.
Gold standard for confirmation, but invasive and not first.
Assesses his COPD, not pulmonary pressure.

steps.x: C: Echocardiogram. Initial test for PH = echocardiogram; confirm with right heart catheterisation.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with suspected idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension has an echocardiogram showing a raised estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure and a dilated right ventricle. Lung function and CT are normal. The specialist centre wants to confirm the diagnosis and directly measure pulmonary pressures before starting targeted therapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Right heart catheterisation directly measures pulmonary pressures and is the gold standard diagnostic test.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
Gold standard needed.

elim: Assesses RV structure but does not directly measure pressure.
Looks for emboli; does not measure pressure.
Screens for thromboembolic disease, not confirmation of PH.

steps.x: D: Right heart catheterisation. Gold standard for PH = right heart catheterisation.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has echocardiography showing pulmonary hypertension with a dilated right ventricle. She had a pulmonary embolism 2 years ago and stopped anticoagulation after 6 months. She has never smoked and her spirometry is normal. The team wants to look for a cause that can be treated.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CT pulmonary angiography is a supporting test that shows chronic thromboembolic obstruction, a treatable cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Previous PE; looking for chronic thromboembolism.

elim: Not a test for pulmonary vascular disease.
Non-specific and cannot show chronic clot.
Looks for DVT, not chronic pulmonary arterial obstruction.
She already has the diagnosis; it will not show the cause.

steps.x: B: CT pulmonary angiography. Always look for and treat the underlying cause; CTPA for thromboembolic disease.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with severe COPD has a loud P2 and ankle oedema. His oxygen saturation is 87% breathing air and his JVP is raised 4 cm. He has an echocardiogram to assess for pulmonary hypertension.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
o: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with outflow obstruction
Dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 25%
Dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle with raised pulmonary pressure
Pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse
questions.e: Raised RV afterload causes RV hypertrophy then dilatation, and the echo estimates a raised pulmonary artery pressure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
COPD with signs of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.
C: Dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle with raised pulmonary pressure. Echo in PH: big, thick RV and high estimated pulmonary pressure.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with severe COPD and a BMI of 38 kg/m² has a raised JVP, loud P2 and oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography was attempted but the images were non-diagnostic because of hyperinflated lungs and body habitus. Pulmonary hypertension must be confirmed or excluded.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Right heart catheterisation directly measures pulmonary pressures and confirms the diagnosis when echo is inconclusive.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
Echo failed; need a definitive test.
D: Right heart catheterisation. Echo first; right heart catheterisation is the gold standard confirmation.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has 6 months of exertional breathlessness. Her GP arranged a chest X-ray. She has a loud P2 and no crackles. Her oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air and her ECG shows right axis deviation. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged central pulmonary arteries and an enlarged cardiac silhouette.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Prominent pulmonary arteries on X-ray and right axis deviation suggest PH; echocardiogram is the initial investigation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
Supporting tests point to PH.

elim: A supporting test once PH is shown.

steps.x: C: Echocardiogram. CXR and ECG support; echo is first; RHC confirms.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with pulmonary hypertension from COPD has 2 weeks of worsening bilateral ankle swelling. Her JVP is raised 5 cm and she has pitting oedema to the knees. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Her lungs sound unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Supportive treatment: diuretics for fluid overload, oxygen only if hypoxic.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Fluid overloaded but not hypoxic.

elim: Targeted PAH therapy, not used first for fluid overload in COPD-related PH.
For severe refractory disease, not first-line.

steps.x: C: Furosemide. Diuretics if overloaded; oxygen only if hypoxic.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with COPD and pulmonary hypertension is reviewed in clinic when stable. He stopped smoking 5 years ago. He has no oedema. His oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air at rest on two visits 3 weeks apart.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: He is persistently hypoxic, so oxygen is given; it reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: 86% breathing air at rest on two visits
steps.x: Chronic hypoxia without fluid overload.

elim: Targeted PAH therapy; not used for COPD-related PH.
Not the treatment for hypoxic PH from COPD.

steps.x: C: Long-term oxygen therapy. Oxygen if hypoxic; diuretics if overloaded.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension confirmed on right heart catheterisation. She is breathless on climbing one flight of stairs. She has no fluid overload and her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. The specialist centre starts a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor.
questions.q: Which drug has been started?
questions.e: Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor pulmonary vasodilator used in PAH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug has been started?
PAH needing a vasodilator.

elim: A beta-blocker; not a pulmonary vasodilator.
A nitrate, not a PDE-5 inhibitor and not used for PAH.
An ACE inhibitor; not a PAH therapy.

steps.x: E: Sildenafil. Pulmonary vasodilators (PDE-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues) treat PAH.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and has started an endothelin receptor antagonist and a pulmonary vasodilator under a specialist centre. She has no history of bleeding. The consultant explains that one further medicine is recommended for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional medicine?
questions.e: In PAH, anticoagulation is given alongside vasodilators and endothelin receptor antagonists.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional medicine?
PAH on targeted therapy.
E: Warfarin. PAH: anticoagulation + vasodilators + endothelin receptor antagonists.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has severe pulmonary hypertension from interstitial lung disease. Over 6 months he has become breathless at rest despite oxygen, diuretics and specialist therapy. He is otherwise fit with no other organ disease. His oxygen saturation is 84% on 4 L/min oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Severe pulmonary hypertension refractory to treatment should be referred for lung transplantation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: breathless at rest despite oxygen, diuretics and specialist therapy
steps.x: Severe and refractory despite maximal therapy.

elim: Does not change the course of severe refractory PH.
He is not described as overloaded; it does not treat the disease.
Beta-blockers can worsen right heart failure in PH.

steps.x: D: Referral for lung transplantation. Severe or refractory PH = refer for lung transplantation.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with COPD has pulmonary hypertension on echocardiography. She still smokes 20 cigarettes a day and uses only a salbutamol inhaler. Her oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air and she has no oedema. She asks whether there is a tablet to lower her lung pressures.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Optimise COPD treatment and stop smoking
questions.e: Always treat the underlying cause: in COPD-related PH, stop smoking and optimise the lung disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
Untreated cause.

elim: Targeted PAH therapy; not for PH caused by COPD.
Not for disease that has not been optimised.
Not the answer when the cause is untreated lung disease.

steps.x: B: Optimise COPD treatment and stop smoking. PH management always includes treating the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has pulmonary hypertension on echocardiography with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. He has orthopnoea and ankle oedema. He takes only furosemide. Right heart catheterisation is not planned. His BP is 132/80 mmHg and potassium is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease is treated by treating the cause: optimise heart failure therapy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
PH from undertreated LV failure.

elim: PAH therapy; not for PH from left heart disease.
Not for PH from untreated left heart failure.
Not used to treat PH from left heart disease.

steps.x: C: Optimise heart failure treatment. Treat the underlying cause of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with pulmonary hypertension from COPD has 1 month of right upper quadrant discomfort and ankle swelling. His liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin and tender. His JVP is raised 6 cm. He drinks no alcohol and hepatitis serology is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hepatomegaly?
o: Hepatic congestion from right ventricular failure
questions.e: RV failure raises systemic venous pressure, congesting the liver: raised JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hepatomegaly?
Hepatomegaly with a raised JVP.

elim: No suggestion of malignancy; the JVP is raised.

steps.x: B: Hepatic congestion from right ventricular failure. Cor pulmonale: raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension has cardiac MRI. It shows a thick-walled right ventricle that is now beginning to dilate, with a normal left ventricle. Her coronary arteries are normal. She asks why her right ventricle has changed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these changes?
o: Increased right ventricular preload from volume overload
questions.e: Raised pulmonary arterial pressure increases RV afterload, causing hypertrophy, then dilatation and failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of these changes?
RV hypertrophy then dilatation.

elim: The driver is pressure (afterload), not volume.
No viral illness; changes are confined to the RV.

steps.x: A: Increased right ventricular afterload. PH raises RV afterload: hypertrophy, dilatation, failure (cor pulmonale).

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with long-standing severe COPD and chronic hypoxia had ankle oedema, a raised JVP and a loud P2 for several years before dying of right heart failure. At post-mortem his small pulmonary arteries are examined under the microscope. His left ventricle and coronary arteries are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological finding in his small pulmonary arteries?
questions.e: Sustained hypoxic vasoconstriction causes remodelling: medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis, raising pulmonary vascular resistance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely histological finding in his small pulmonary arteries?
Chronic hypoxic lung disease.

elim: A feature of large systemic arteries.

steps.x: E: Medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis. Hypoxia: vasoconstriction, then remodelling, then raised PVR.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with COPD and pulmonary hypertension is started on long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxia. Her respiratory nurse explains that, used for at least 15 hours a day, it slows the rise in her pulmonary pressures. Her PaO2 on air is 7.1 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this benefit?
questions.e: Hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and raised vascular resistance; correcting hypoxia removes that stimulus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of this benefit?

clues: slows the rise in her pulmonary pressures
steps.x: Why oxygen lowers pulmonary pressure.
D: Reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. In lung-disease PH, oxygen reverses hypoxic vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man had a large pulmonary embolism 2 years ago. He now has progressive breathlessness, a loud P2 and a raised JVP. CT pulmonary angiography shows organised chronic clot and webs in several lobar arteries. His spirometry and left ventricular function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pulmonary hypertension?
o: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from lung disease
Increased pulmonary blood flow from a shunt
Unresolved emboli obstructing the pulmonary arteries
Vasoconstriction from excess endothelin with no cause
questions.e: Chronic thromboembolic PH results from unresolved emboli obstructing the pulmonary vasculature and raising resistance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pulmonary hypertension?
Old PE with residual clot.

elim: That describes idiopathic PAH; here clot is shown.

steps.x: D: Unresolved emboli obstructing the pulmonary arteries. CTEPH = unresolved emboli raise pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension starts sildenafil. After 3 months she can walk further and her estimated pulmonary artery pressure has fallen. She has no side effects apart from mild headache and flushing. She asks how the tablet works.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of her drug?
o: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 to relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle
questions.e: Sildenafil inhibits PDE-5, raising cGMP and relaxing pulmonary vascular smooth muscle to lower pulmonary vascular resistance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of her drug?
A PDE-5 inhibitor lowered pressure.

elim: That is how prostacyclin analogues work.
A beta-blocker; not a pulmonary vasodilator.

steps.x: D: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 to relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle. PDE-5 inhibitors and prostacyclin analogues reduce pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension is started on bosentan by a specialist centre, alongside anticoagulation. His liver function is monitored monthly. He asks how the new drug lowers the pressure in his lungs.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of bosentan?
o: Blocks endothelin receptors on pulmonary vascular smooth muscle
Blocks loop of Henle sodium reabsorption
questions.e: Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist, blocking endothelin-1 vasoconstriction and lowering pulmonary vascular resistance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of bosentan?
Bosentan in PAH.
B: Blocks endothelin receptors on pulmonary vascular smooth muscle. Endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan) block endothelin-mediated vasoconstriction.
